title: Call for Papers: IEEPA at 50
text:
Scott R. Anderson

Over the last half century, the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) has become one of the most consequential grants of presidential power in U.S. foreign affairs. When President Jimmy Carter signed IEEPA into law on December 28, 1977, as part of a wave of post-Watergate bills, Congress intended the Act to narrow the use of older emergency economic powers. But in practice, the Executive Branch has interpreted IEEPA broadly and invoked it for a far wider range of purposes than its predecessors. IEEPA has formed the legal foundation for most U.S. sanctions programs, as well as U.S. export control programs when their own authorizing statute lapsed. And over the past decade, Presidents have deployed a growing array of new IEEPA-based measures, including to regulate cross-border data transfers, U.S. investment overseas, Chinese technology equipment use, and Venezuelan oil revenues. Soon after taking office, President Trump relied on IEEPA to impose sweeping global tariffs, putting the statute at the center of litigation that reached the Supreme Court. In early 2026, the Court held that IEEPA’s authority to “regulate…any…importation or exportation of…property” does not include the power to impose tariffs. Whether and how the Court’s reasoning might extend beyond tariffs remains an open question.    Georgetown Law’s Institute of International Economic Law (IIEL) and Lawfare will convene a symposium in Washington, D.C., next fall—on Thursday, October 28, 2027—to examine this landmark law’s first 50 years and what comes next.In connection with the symposium, Lawfare and IIEL invite proposals for short research papers (4,000 to 8,000 words) exploring IEEPA’s past, present, and future. Selected papers will be published in a Lawfare series, and several authors will be invited to present their work on panels at the symposium. Paper proposals are particularly welcome on, but need not be limited to, the following themes:IEEPA law and practice in historical perspective;Congress, the courts, and the separation of emergency economic powers; IEEPA, the Constitution, and individual rights, including free speech and due process;War, peace, and IEEPA as a foreign policy tool;IEEPA, industrial policy, and emerging technologies; andComparative and international perspectives on—and reactions to—the use of IEEPA.IIEL and Lawfare especially welcome new historical perspectives as well as forward-looking analyses that diagnose where the law is heading, how its assumptions have been tested, and whether and how it should change. Academics, practitioners, and policymakers are all encouraged to submit. To be considered, please send a 500-word abstract and a copy of your curriculum vitae to lawiiel@georgetown.edu by January 15, 2027.Additional information on both the symposium and the paper series will be posted to http://www.lawfaremedia.org and https://www.law.georgetown.edu/iiel as it becomes available.

Scott R. Anderson is a Senior Editor at Lawfare and General Counsel of the Lawfare Institute. He is also a Senior Fellow in Governance Studies at the Brookings Institution and a Non-resident Senior Fellow in the National Security Law Program at Columbia Law School. He previously served as an Attorney-Adviser in the Office of the Legal Adviser at the U.S. Department of State and as the legal advisor for the U.S. Embassy in Baghdad, Iraq.
